title: Gastrointestinal Embryology
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)

overview.intro: This chapter follows the gut from a simple endodermal tube to the adult digestive tract and its glands. It covers the three gut divisions and their arteries, midgut herniation and rotation, separation of the esophagus from the airway, budding of the liver and pancreas, colonization of the gut wall by neural crest, and recanalization of the duodenum. Board questions usually describe a newborn with vomiting, drooling, a midline sac, or delayed meconium and ask which developmental step failed. They also use the gut divisions to explain blood supply and why visceral pain is felt in the epigastric, periumbilical, or suprapubic region. If you know what each step normally does, every defect follows from it.
prerequisites: Germ layers and embryonic folding in weeks 3 and 4
Ventral branches of the abdominal aorta
Organization of sympathetic, parasympathetic, and visceral afferent fibers (NE-9)

connections.how: The celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric territories are the foregut, midgut, and hindgut, and their junctions are the watershed zones.

connections.to: The gut in the body cavities (GI-4)
connections.how: Rotation and fixation of the mesenteries explain which organs end up secondarily retroperitoneal.
The lung bud and trachea arise from the same foregut tube as the esophagus, so their separation defects are shared.
The neural crest derived enteric plexuses are the circuits that coordinate peristalsis and secretion.
Atresias, malrotation, abdominal wall defects, and Hirschsprung disease are developmental failures described here.

sections.title: Gut tube divisions, their arteries, and referred visceral pain

blocks.text: During week 4, cephalocaudal and lateral folding of the embryo draws the dorsal part of the yolk sac inside as the primitive gut. Endoderm forms the epithelial lining and the secretory cells of the liver and pancreas; the surrounding splanchnic mesoderm forms the connective tissue, smooth muscle, and visceral peritoneum. The tube is closed cranially by the oropharyngeal membrane and caudally by the cloacal membrane, and the midgut stays open to the yolk sac through the vitelline duct.

Each abdominal division is supplied by one unpaired ventral branch of the aorta, and these three arteries develop from the vitelline arteries that once supplied the yolk sac. Because each artery grows with its segment, the arterial borders are the embryologic borders. The foregut ends just distal to the major duodenal papilla, where the bile duct enters, and the midgut ends at the junction of the proximal two thirds and distal third of the transverse colon. The junctions receive blood from both neighbors, such as the pancreatic head through the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries. Where territories meet, as at the splenic flexure, collateral flow is thin and the wall is vulnerable to ischemia when perfusion falls (GI-5).

blocks.title: The three gut divisions
rows: Abdominal esophagus, stomach, duodenum to the major papilla, liver, gallbladder, pancreas
Duodenum distal to the papilla, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal two thirds of transverse colon
Distal third of transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal above the pectinate line
blocks.caption: The pharynx and thoracic esophagus are also foregut but take blood from other arteries. The spleen is supplied by the celiac trunk but is mesodermal, forming in the dorsal mesogastrium, so it is not a gut derivative.

blocks.text: Visceral pain fibers from most of the gut run back along the sympathetic splanchnic nerves to the spinal segments that supplied each division in the embryo: roughly T5 to T9 for the foregut, T10 to T11 for the midgut, and T12 to L2 for the hindgut. The exception is the distal sigmoid colon and rectum, whose pain fibers travel with the pelvic splanchnic nerves to S2 to S4. In the dorsal horn they converge on neurons that also receive input from skin of the same segments, so the brain projects the sensation onto those dermatomes. The umbilicus lies in the T10 dermatome, which is why midgut pain is periumbilical.

Visceral afferents are sparse and bilateral and respond to distension, ischemia, and inflammation rather than cutting. Visceral pain is therefore dull, cramping, poorly localized, felt in the midline, and often accompanied by nausea, sweating, and pallor. When inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, which is supplied by somatic nerves of the body wall, the pain becomes sharp and localizes over the organ.

blocks.title: How visceral pain is referred
steps: Distension, ischemia, or inflammation stimulates visceral afferents
Fibers travel with sympathetic splanchnic nerves
Enter the cord at the segment of that gut division
Converge on dorsal horn neurons shared with skin input
Brain localizes pain to the midline dermatome
blocks.caption: Convergence of visceral and somatic input on the same spinal neurons explains why gut pain is felt on the body wall.

blocks.title: Why appendicitis pain moves
blocks.text: Obstruction of the appendix lumen distends its wall. The appendix is midgut, so its afferents enter the cord at about T10, and the first pain is dull, periumbilical, and accompanied by nausea. Over several hours inflammation reaches the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum in the right iliac fossa, so the pain shifts to the right lower quadrant and becomes sharp, localized, and worse with movement.

sections.title: Midgut herniation, rotation, and their failures

blocks.text: The midgut forms a U shaped primary intestinal loop suspended by dorsal mesentery. The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) runs in that mesentery as the axis of the loop, and the vitelline duct attaches at its apex. The cranial limb becomes the distal duodenum, jejunum, and most of the ileum; the caudal limb becomes the distal ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and proximal two thirds of the transverse colon. A small swelling on the caudal limb, the cecal bud, marks the future cecum.

In week 6 the loop lengthens quickly while the large liver and the mesonephric kidneys fill the small abdominal cavity. Lacking room, the loop passes into the extraembryonic coelom within the umbilical cord. This physiologic herniation is normal. While in the cord, the loop turns 90 degrees counterclockwise, viewed from the front, around the SMA. Around week 10, as liver growth slows, the mesonephros regresses, and the abdomen enlarges, the loops return. The jejunum returns first and settles on the left, and the loop completes a further 180 degrees, for 270 degrees in total. The cecum returns last, lies at first below the liver, and then descends to the right iliac fossa.

steps: Week 6: midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord

Colonic mesenteries fuse with the posterior wall
blocks.caption: Rotation viewed from the front. Fusion of the colonic mesenteries makes the ascending and descending colon secondarily retroperitoneal.

blocks.text: Normal rotation places the third part of the duodenum behind the SMA, with the duodenojejunal junction left of midline, and gives the small bowel mesentery a long diagonal root that keeps the bowel from twisting.

In malrotation the loop stops short of 270 degrees. With nonrotation (only the first 90 degrees) the small bowel lies on the right and the colon on the left. With incomplete rotation the cecum stays high near the midline, and peritoneal (Ladd) bands run from it across the second part of the duodenum to the right posterior wall, where they can compress the duodenum. The dangerous feature is the mesentery: it stays short, narrow, and centered on the SMA, so the whole midgut can twist around the vessel. This midgut volvulus obstructs the bowel and occludes the SMA and superior mesenteric vein, threatening ischemia from the distal duodenum to the transverse colon. It most often presents in the first month of life, though it can occur at any age, with sudden bilious vomiting, since the block lies below the papilla. A contrast study shows the duodenojejunal junction right of midline.

If the herniated loops fail to return, the infant has an omphalocele: bowel, and sometimes liver, in a midline sac into which the cord inserts. It often accompanies trisomies 13 and 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and cardiac and neural tube defects.

blocks.title: Omphalocele and gastroschisis
rows: Lateral body wall fails to close
Beside the umbilicus, usually on the right
None; bowel bathed in amniotic fluid
Uncommon; bowel often thickened and inflamed
blocks.caption: Both raise maternal serum alpha fetoprotein.

blocks.predict: A newborn's contrast study shows the duodenojejunal junction to the right of the spine. Which segments of bowel are at risk of infarction, and which are spared?
blocks.explain: The narrow mesentery of malrotation lets the midgut twist around the SMA, so the whole SMA territory from the distal duodenum to the distal transverse colon is at risk, while the hindgut supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery is spared.

sections.title: Separation of the esophagus from the airway

blocks.text: Early in week 4 the respiratory (laryngotracheal) diverticulum buds from the ventral wall of the foregut just below the pharynx. As it grows caudally, longitudinal tracheoesophageal ridges grow in from the lateral walls of the foregut and fuse in the midline to form the tracheoesophageal septum. The septum divides the tube into a ventral part, which becomes the larynx, trachea, and lung buds, and a dorsal part, which becomes the esophagus. The two remain connected only at the laryngeal inlet.

blocks.title: Normal division of the foregut
steps: Respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut
Tracheoesophageal ridges grow in from the lateral walls
Ridges fuse into the tracheoesophageal septum
Ventral tube becomes larynx, trachea, and lung buds
Dorsal tube becomes the esophagus
blocks.caption: Airway and esophagus share one origin, so a faulty septum leaves them joined or leaves the esophagus interrupted.

blocks.text: The esophagus is short at first and lengthens quickly as the heart and lungs descend into the thorax. Its epithelium proliferates and partly fills the lumen before recanalizing, and its muscle comes from the surrounding mesenchyme: striated in the upper esophagus and smooth in the lower esophagus, with a mixed zone between. The vagus supplies both, the striated part directly and the smooth part through the enteric plexus. If the esophagus fails to lengthen enough, part of the stomach is pulled through the diaphragm as a congenital hiatal hernia.

When the septum deviates posteriorly, or the dorsal foregut wall is pushed forward, the division is incomplete. The result is esophageal atresia, in which the esophagus ends blindly, a tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF), an abnormal channel between the esophagus and trachea, or both. The defect occurs in about 1 in 3,000 births. In esophageal atresia, swallowed amniotic fluid cannot reach the intestine, where it is normally absorbed and returned to the mother through the placenta, so polyhydramnios is common. About half of affected infants have other anomalies, and the defect belongs to the VACTERL association: vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb anomalies.

blocks.caption: Gas below the diaphragm means the lower esophagus connects to the airway; a gasless abdomen means it does not.

blocks.predict: A newborn drools, cannot pass a feeding tube, and has no gas anywhere in the abdomen on radiograph. Which form of the defect is present?
blocks.explain: Isolated esophageal atresia without a distal fistula. Without a connection between the trachea and lower esophagus, swallowed or inhaled air cannot reach the stomach, so the bowel is gasless.

blocks.text: The liver begins in weeks 3 to 4 as the hepatic diverticulum, an endodermal outgrowth from the ventral wall of the distal foregut where the duodenum will form. It grows into the septum transversum. There its endodermal cords become hepatocytes and the lining of the intrahepatic bile ducts, and they surround the vitelline and umbilical veins, which break up to form the hepatic sinusoids. Mesoderm of the septum transversum forms the connective tissue of the liver, and the ventral mesentery derived from it becomes the lesser omentum and the falciform ligament. Hepatocytes begin to secrete bile at about week 12.

The stalk joining the liver bud to the foregut narrows to become the bile duct, and a small ventral outgrowth from it forms the gallbladder and cystic duct. The bile duct first opens on the ventral wall of the duodenum; when the duodenum rotates to the right and becomes C shaped, its opening is carried to the dorsomedial wall, so the adult bile duct passes behind the duodenum. In biliary atresia the extrahepatic ducts are destroyed by a progressive inflammatory and fibrosing process around the time of birth, rather than by simple failure of a developmental step. Because bile cannot reach the gut, infants develop conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, dark urine, and pale stools in the first weeks, followed by biliary cirrhosis.

The pancreas forms from two endodermal buds of the duodenum. The dorsal bud grows into the dorsal mesentery; the ventral bud lies beside the bile duct. When the duodenum rotates, the ventral bud travels with the bile duct around the back of the duodenum and comes to lie below and behind the dorsal bud. The parenchyma fuses, and the duct systems join so that the main pancreatic duct drains with the bile duct at the major papilla. Islets develop from the same endoderm in the third month.

blocks.text: Two defects follow from this sequence. In annular pancreas the ventral bud is bifid; one half migrates normally while the other passes around the opposite side of the duodenum, so a ring of pancreatic tissue encircles the second part of the duodenum. The ring can narrow or obstruct the duodenum in a newborn or present later in life, and it is associated with Down syndrome and duodenal atresia. In pancreas divisum the parenchyma fuses but the ducts do not. The dorsal duct then drains most of the gland through the small minor papilla, while the ventral duct drains only the uncinate process and lower head. It is the most common congenital anomaly of the pancreas and is usually silent, but in a minority the high flow through a narrow opening is thought to raise ductal pressure and contribute to recurrent acute pancreatitis.

sections.title: Neural crest and the enteric nervous system

blocks.text: The enteric nervous system comes from neural crest. Most of it arises from vagal neural crest at the level of the hindbrain, with a smaller sacral crest contribution to the hindgut. These cells enter the foregut and migrate in a cranial to caudal wave through the gut mesenchyme, reaching the distal rectum during the early fetal period. They first form the myenteric plexus between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers, and some then move inward to form the submucosal plexus.

blocks.title: Cells that control the gut wall
rows: Secretion, absorption, and local blood flow
blocks.caption: Enteric neurons include excitatory neurons that release acetylcholine and inhibitory neurons that release nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).

blocks.text: Migration depends on signaling. Gut mesenchyme secretes glial cell line derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), which binds the RET receptor tyrosine kinase on crest cells and drives their survival, proliferation, and migration. Endothelin 3 acting on the endothelin B receptor (EDNRB) keeps precursors dividing so the pool is large enough to colonize the whole gut, and the transcription factor SOX10 is needed for the crest cells to survive. Melanocytes also come from neural crest, so EDNRB, endothelin 3, and SOX10 mutations can combine aganglionosis with patchy depigmentation and deafness (Waardenburg syndrome type 4).

Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) results when the wave stops before reaching the end of the gut. Loss of function mutations in RET are the most common identified cause. Because colonization proceeds cranial to caudal, the aganglionic segment always begins at the internal anal sphincter and extends proximally a variable distance, most often only through the rectosigmoid. It affects about 1 in 5,000 births, is about four times more common in boys, and about 10% of cases occur in children with Down syndrome.

blocks.title: From RET mutation to megacolon
steps: RET loss of function reduces GDNF signaling
Neural crest wave stops before the distal bowel
Distal segment lacks myenteric and submucosal ganglia
No inhibitory NO and VIP neurons, so segment cannot relax
Peristalsis stops at the narrow segment: functional obstruction
Proximal normal colon dilates and hypertrophies
blocks.caption: The diseased segment is the narrow one; the dilated colon above it is normal bowel stretched by retained stool.

blocks.text: The aganglionic segment stays tonically contracted, and the rectoanal inhibitory reflex, relaxation of the internal sphincter when the rectum is distended, is absent. Newborns fail to pass meconium in the first 48 hours and develop abdominal distension and vomiting; a rectal examination may release an explosive gush of gas and stool. A contrast enema shows a narrow distal segment and a transition zone to dilated colon. Rectal suction biopsy shows no ganglion cells in the submucosa and thickened acetylcholinesterase positive nerve fibers from extrinsic nerves. Enterocolitis from stasis is the most feared complication. Acquired megacolon in Chagas disease is the microbiologic parallel: Trypanosoma cruzi destroys ganglia that had formed normally.

blocks.predict: Could a failure of neural crest migration leave the transverse colon aganglionic while the rectum has normal ganglia?
blocks.explain: Essentially no. Crest cells colonize the gut from cranial to caudal, so any arrest leaves the most distal bowel uncolonized. The rectum is always involved, and skip lesions are extremely rare.
blocks.check: Compare with the description of migration and the Hirschsprung paragraph.

blocks.text: The duodenum forms from the end of the foregut and the beginning of the midgut, with the junction just distal to the opening of the bile duct, which is why it receives both celiac and superior mesenteric blood. As the stomach rotates, the duodenum becomes C shaped, swings to the right, and most of it becomes secondarily retroperitoneal when its mesentery fuses with the posterior wall. During the second month its epithelium proliferates so rapidly that it fills the lumen. Vacuoles then form within the epithelial plug and coalesce, and the lumen is restored by the end of the embryonic period.

If recanalization fails, the duodenum is completely closed (atresia) or narrowed by a web or diaphragm (stenosis). Most duodenal atresias lie in the second part just distal to the major papilla, so bile enters the obstructed segment and the vomitus is bilious; a lesion above the papilla gives nonbilious vomiting. The fetus cannot carry swallowed amniotic fluid to the absorptive intestine, so polyhydramnios is common. A plain radiograph shows the double bubble: gas in the stomach and in the dilated proximal duodenum, with no gas beyond in complete atresia. About 30% of affected infants have trisomy 21, and annular pancreas, malrotation, and cardiac defects often coexist.

Atresia of the jejunum and ileum has a different cause. These segments become atretic after an intrauterine vascular accident, such as volvulus or occlusion of a mesenteric branch, that leads to ischemic necrosis and resorption of a segment of bowel. They produce several dilated loops, more distension, and are not associated with Down syndrome. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is not a developmental failure; the pyloric muscle thickens after birth.

blocks.title: Reading a double bubble
blocks.text: A newborn whose mother had polyhydramnios vomits bile stained fluid a few hours after the first feed. The abdomen is not distended, and the radiograph shows a double bubble with no gas beyond. Bile places the block below the major papilla. The two bubbles are the stomach and the dilated proximal duodenum, and the absence of distal gas means the obstruction is complete rather than a stenosis. Polyhydramnios shows that swallowed fluid never reached the absorptive bowel, and the flat abdomen shows the block is high. This is duodenal atresia from failed recanalization of the second part, and the infant should be examined for features of trisomy 21. If gas were present beyond the duodenum, malrotation with volvulus would have to be considered, because a twist can be partial and still strangle the entire midgut.

integration.text: Each defect in this chapter is a normal step that failed, and the step tells you the anatomy, the signs, and the associations. Pathology explains the timing and pattern of each defect: failed recanalization gives duodenal atresia, while a vascular accident gives jejunoileal atresia, and failed return gives omphalocele, while failed body wall closure gives gastroschisis. Genetics and syndromes link the gut to the rest of the body, as with trisomy 21 in duodenal atresia, annular pancreas, and Hirschsprung disease, and the VACTERL association with tracheoesophageal fistula.

Physiology and microbiology show why these structures matter after birth. The enteric plexuses are the circuits that coordinate peristalsis, and losing their inhibitory neurons, whether by failed migration or by Trypanosoma cruzi infection, produces the same functional obstruction and dilation. The limits of embryologic reasoning are real: the timing of weeks and the frequencies of associated anomalies vary between sources, and conditions such as biliary atresia and pyloric stenosis appear in newborns but are not simple failures of a developmental step.

summary: Foregut, midgut, and hindgut are supplied by the celiac trunk, superior mesenteric artery, and inferior mesenteric artery; the borders lie just distal to the major papilla and at the distal third of the transverse colon.

Visceral pain travels with sympathetic afferents to the spinal segments of each division and is referred to the epigastrium, umbilicus, or suprapubic region; it localizes only when the parietal peritoneum is involved.
The midgut herniates into the cord in week 6, rotates 270 degrees counterclockwise around the SMA (90 degrees outside, 180 degrees during return), and returns by about week 10.
Malrotation leaves a narrow mesentery that can twist around the SMA, causing bilious vomiting and ischemia of the whole midgut; Ladd bands can compress the duodenum.
Omphalocele is failed return of the physiologic hernia into a sac of amnion and peritoneum, often with aneuploidy; gastroschisis is an uncovered body wall defect beside the umbilicus.
The tracheoesophageal septum separates the ventral airway from the dorsal esophagus; posterior deviation gives atresia, fistula, or both, most often a blind upper pouch with a distal fistula.

The ventral pancreatic bud rotates behind the duodenum with the bile duct; a bifid ventral bud gives annular pancreas, and failed duct fusion gives pancreas divisum with drainage through the minor papilla.

Neural crest colonizes the gut cranial to caudal under GDNF and RET signaling, so Hirschsprung disease always involves the rectum and produces a narrow aganglionic segment below a dilated normal colon.

Failed recanalization of the second part of the duodenum gives bilious vomiting, polyhydramnios, a double bubble, and a strong association with trisomy 21; jejunoileal atresia follows vascular accidents.

verify: Spinal levels for visceral afferents differ between sources (for example foregut T5 to T9 or T6 to T9, hindgut T12 to L2 or L1 to L2), as does the exact level of the pelvic pain line in the sigmoid colon; confirm the ranges NABNE expects.

Timing differs slightly between texts for the hepatic diverticulum (week 3 or 4), return of the midgut (week 10 or later), duodenal recanalization (second month), and arrival of neural crest in the distal rectum (quoted from week 7 to week 12).

Frequencies are approximate and vary by series: atresia with distal fistula about 85 to 90% of esophageal atresia cases; trisomy 21 in about 30% of duodenal atresia; Down syndrome in about 10% of Hirschsprung cases; Hirschsprung about 1 in 5,000 births; esophageal atresia about 1 in 3,000 births.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Ladd bands, Auerbach and Meissner plexuses, and Waardenburg syndrome type 4, or only the descriptive terms.
The causes of biliary atresia remain under study; the inflammatory, fibro-obliterative model is the current consensus.
